title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LV
paragraphs:
Hath she her faults? I would you had them too.
They are the fruity must of soundest wine;
Or say, they are regenerating fire
Such as hath turned the dense black element
Into a crystal pathway for the sun.

If youth is a time of hope, that often means only that older people have hopes for us. No one is more likely than the young to believe that their feelings, their farewells, and their resolutions can never be repeated. Every crisis feels final simply because it is new. We are told that even the oldest people in Peru are still disturbed by earthquakes; but they probably look beyond each shock and remember that there will be plenty more.

Dorothea was still at that age when eyes framed by long, thick lashes can emerge from a shower of tears as fresh and untired as a newly opened passion-flower. To her, that morning’s farewell to Will Ladislaw seemed to end their personal connection. He was disappearing into an unknown stretch of years, and if he ever returned, he would be a different man. She had no idea of his actual thoughts: his proud determination to disprove in advance any suspicion that he was a penniless adventurer pursuing a rich woman. She had readily explained everything he did by assuming that Mr. Casaubon’s codicil seemed to him, as it did to her, a brutal, cruel ban on any continuing friendship between them. Their youthful pleasure in talking together, in saying things no one else would have cared to hear, was over forever, a treasure belonging to the past. Precisely for that reason, she let herself dwell on it without restraint. That unique happiness was dead too, and in its dark, silent room she could release a passionate grief that astonished even her. For the first time, she took the miniature off the wall and kept it in front of her. She liked to bring together in her thoughts the woman who had been judged too harshly and the grandson whom both her heart and her reason defended. Could anyone who has delighted in a woman’s tenderness blame her for cupping the small oval picture in her hand, making a bed for it there, and resting her cheek against it, as though this could comfort those unjustly condemned? She did not yet understand that Love had briefly visited her, like a dream just before waking, his wings bright with the colors of dawn. She did not know it was to Love that she was sobbing her farewell, as his image vanished before the blameless severity of inescapable daylight. She felt only that something in her life was irreparably wrong, something lost; and this made her thoughts about the future turn all the more readily into resolutions. Passionate people, eager to build their future lives, are apt to pledge themselves to making their own visions real.

One day Dorothea went to Freshitt, as she had promised, to stay overnight and watch the baby being washed. Mrs. Cadwallader came to dinner; the Rector was away fishing. The evening was warm. Even in the lovely drawing room, whose open window looked down over fine old turf to a lily pond and carefully planted mounds, the heat was enough to make Celia, in her white muslin and loose curls, pity Dodo in her black dress and close-fitting cap. She did not think of this, however, until various proceedings involving the baby were over and her mind was free again. She had been sitting with a fan for some time before she said, in her quiet, throaty voice,
“Dear Dodo, please take that cap off. Your clothes must be making you feel quite ill.”
“I’ve grown so used to it—it’s become a kind of shell,” Dorothea said with a smile. “Without it I feel rather naked and exposed.”

“I insist on seeing you without it. Just looking at it makes us all hot,” said Celia. She put down her fan and went over to Dorothea. The little woman in white muslin made a pretty picture as she undid the widow’s cap on her more majestic sister’s head and tossed it onto a chair. Sir James entered just as the coils and braids of dark brown hair were freed. He looked at the uncovered head and gave a satisfied “Ah!”
“That was my doing, James,” Celia said. “Dodo needn’t be such a slave to mourning. She needn’t wear that cap with her friends anymore.”
“My dear Celia,” Lady Chettam said, “a widow has to stay in mourning for at least a year.”
“Unless she marries again before the year’s up,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, who rather enjoyed shocking her good friend the Dowager. Annoyed, Sir James bent forward to play with Celia’s Maltese dog.

“I hope that very seldom happens,” said Lady Chettam, in a voice intended to prevent it. “None of our friends ever did such a thing except Mrs. Beevor, and Lord Grinsell was deeply distressed by it. Her first husband was objectionable, which made it all the more extraordinary. And she paid dearly for it. They said Captain Beevor pulled her about by her hair and pointed loaded pistols at her.”

“Well, if she chose the wrong man!” said Mrs. Cadwallader, now feeling thoroughly mischievous. “Then marriage is always a bad business, whether it’s the first or the second. Having come first isn’t much of a recommendation in a husband who has nothing else to recommend him. I’d sooner have a good second husband than a mediocre first.”
“My dear, you let that clever tongue of yours run away with you,” said Lady Chettam. “I’m sure you would be the very last woman to remarry too soon if our dear Rector were taken from us.”

“Oh, I won’t make promises. It might be necessary to save money. Remarrying is permitted, I suppose; otherwise we might as well be Hindus as Christians. Naturally, if a woman accepts the wrong man, she must live with the consequences, and if she does it twice she deserves what she gets. But if she can marry good birth, good looks, and courage, the sooner she does it the better.”
“I consider this a very unfortunate choice of conversation,” said Sir James, looking disgusted. “Let’s talk about something else.”

“Please don’t change it for my sake, Sir James,” said Dorothea. She was determined to use this opportunity to put an end to the hints about excellent prospective husbands. “If you’re speaking on my behalf, I assure you that nothing could be more impersonal or less interesting to me than a second marriage. It concerns me no more than a discussion of women going fox-hunting. Whether I admire them for it or not, I won’t be joining them. Please let Mrs. Cadwallader entertain herself with this subject as freely as with any other.”

“My dear Mrs. Casaubon,” said Lady Chettam with her utmost dignity, “I hope you don’t imagine I was referring to you when I mentioned Mrs. Beevor. Hers was simply a case that came to mind. She was Lord Grinsell’s stepdaughter: his second wife was Mrs. Teveroy. There could not possibly have been any reference to you.”
“Of course not,” Celia said. “Nobody chose the subject. It all started with Dodo’s cap. What Mrs. Cadwallader said was perfectly true. A woman couldn’t get married wearing a widow’s cap, James.”

“Quiet, my dear!” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “I won’t misbehave again. I won’t so much as mention Dido or Zenobia. But what shall we talk about? Personally, I object to discussing Human Nature, since that is the nature rectors’ wives happen to have.”

Later that evening, when Mrs. Cadwallader had left, Celia said to Dorothea in private, “Really, Dodo, removing that cap made you yourself again in more than one way. You spoke up exactly as you used to when someone said something you didn’t like. Only I couldn’t quite tell whether you thought James was wrong or Mrs. Cadwallader.”

“Neither of them,” said Dorothea. “James was being considerate of me, but he was wrong to think Mrs. Cadwallader’s remarks upset me. They would only upset me if there were a law forcing me to accept any piece of blood and beauty that she or anyone else recommended.”

“Still, Dodo, if you ever did get married, it would be all the better to have blood and beauty,” Celia said. She was thinking that Mr. Casaubon had been poorly endowed with those gifts, and that Dorothea ought to be warned in time.

“Don’t worry, Kitty. I have quite different ideas for my life. I’m never going to marry again,” Dorothea said, touching her sister’s chin and looking at her with affectionate indulgence. Celia was feeding her baby, and Dorothea had come to wish her good night.
“Really? Absolutely?” said Celia. “No one at all—even if he were quite extraordinary?”

Dorothea slowly shook her head. “No one at all. I have such lovely plans. I’d like to take a large piece of land, drain it, and establish a little community where everyone worked and all the work was properly done. I would know every person there and be their friend. I’m going to consult Mr. Garth at length. He can tell me almost everything I need to know.”
“So you _will_ be happy as long as you have a plan, Dodo?” Celia asked. “Perhaps little Arthur will like making plans when he’s older, and then he can help you.”

That very night Sir James learned that Dorothea was quite determined never to marry anyone and was going to occupy herself with “all sorts of plans,” just as she used to. He said nothing. Privately, he found something repellent in a woman’s marrying for a second time; no possible husband could keep him from feeling that for Dorothea it would be a kind of desecration. He knew the world would find that feeling absurd, especially about a woman of twenty-one. The world’s habit was to discuss a young widow’s remarriage as inevitable and probably imminent, and to smile knowingly when she behaved accordingly. But if Dorothea chose to bind herself to solitude, he felt that such a decision would suit her well.
